CS 351 · Introduction to Natural Language Processing  
Chapter 2 · Tokenization and embeddings
:::

In the previous chapter, we treated “text” as if it could be handed directly to a model. It cannot. A model operates on numbers, so we need to make two decisions:

1. **Tokenization:** which pieces of text will be the model's units?
2. **Representation:** which numbers will stand for those units?

This chapter develops the main ideas and leaves most implementation details to the libraries that solve them well.

```{mermaid}

    B --> C[Token IDs]
    C --> D[Vectors]
```

:::{.callout-note}
## Learning objectives

After this chapter, you should be able to:

1. explain what tokenization does and why it is a modeling decision;
2. describe the limitations of character- and word-level tokenization;
3. explain why subwords are the dominant modern compromise;
4. inspect tokenization with regular expressions, spaCy, and a pretrained model tokenizer;
5. distinguish token identifiers, one-hot vectors, and dense embeddings; and
6. use pretrained embeddings to explore similarity and analogy.
:::

# What is tokenization? {#sec-tokenization}

**Tokenization** segments text into the units a model will process. Each observed unit is a **token**. The set of distinct units known to the model is its **vocabulary**.

```text
Text       "NLP is fascinating!"
Tokens     ["NLP", "is", "fascinating", "!"]
Token IDs  [314, 27, 8921, 4]
```

The identifiers are vocabulary addresses. The number `8921` does not mean that *fascinating* is greater than *NLP*; it only points to a row in a table.

## One string, several valid segmentations

What is the correct tokenization of `don't`?

```text
["don't"]
["do", "n't"]
["don", "'", "t"]
["d", "o", "n", "'", "t"]
```

All four are mechanically possible. A linguistically informed system might preserve the contraction or separate its grammatical components. A subword model might choose reusable character sequences. A character model uses individual symbols.

:::{.callout-important}
Tokenization is not neutral cleanup. It determines the units the model can see, the vocabulary it must store, and the length of every input.
:::

## Token, type, and vocabulary

In the sentence:

> A model is a model.

there are six word/punctuation **tokens**, but fewer distinct **types** because `a` and `model` occur twice. A vocabulary contains types; an input contains token instances.


# Why not tokenize into characters? {#sec-characters}

A character vocabulary is small and can spell any new word.

```text
"token" → ["t", "o", "k", "e", "n"]
```

This avoids unknown words and preserves spelling. It also creates long sequences whose individual units carry little meaning. A model must learn that five distant character decisions together form the familiar concept *token*.

For modern sequence models, length matters: longer sequences require more computation and make long-range relationships harder to manage.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-character-tradeoff
%%| fig-cap: "Character tokenization buys universal coverage at the cost of long sequences."
%%| fig-width: 6.5
flowchart LR
    A[Small vocabulary] --> B[No unknown words]
    B --> C[Long sequences]
    C --> D[More computation]
    C --> E[Meaning spread across many positions]

    classDef benefit fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    classDef cost fill:#f8eeee,stroke:#a34f4f,color:#17364a
    class A,B benefit
    class C,D,E cost
```

# Why not tokenize into words? {#sec-words}

Word tokens are intuitive and produce shorter sequences:

```text
"Tokenization is useful" → ["Tokenization", "is", "useful"]
```

But language continually creates new names, inflections, compounds, technical terms, hashtags, and spelling variants. A fixed vocabulary can never contain every word form.

```text
train        known
trained      perhaps known
retrained    perhaps unknown
retraining   perhaps unknown
```

A word-level system either grows an enormous vocabulary or maps unfamiliar words to a single `<UNK>` token. Both choices waste useful structure.

## The granularity dilemma

| Unit | Vocabulary | Sequence | New words | Main weakness |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Character | Small | Long | Always representable | Meaning is distributed across many positions |
| Word | Very large | Short | Often unknown | Vocabulary cannot cover productive language |
| Subword | Moderate | Moderate | Usually decomposable | Segmentation can be unintuitive |

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-granularity
%%| fig-cap: "Subwords occupy the useful middle ground between character coverage and word efficiency."
%%| fig-width: 7.0
flowchart LR
    C[Characters<br/>small vocabulary<br/>long sequence]
    S[Subwords<br/>balanced compromise]
    W[Words<br/>large vocabulary<br/>short sequence]
    C <--> S <--> W

    classDef edge fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#b48a32,color:#17364a
    classDef middle fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a,stroke-width:3px
    class C,W edge
    class S middle
```

# The modern compromise: subwords {#sec-subwords}

A **subword tokenizer** keeps frequent forms intact and decomposes rarer forms into reusable pieces.

```text
the             → ["the"]
tokenization    → ["token", "ization"]
unhappiness     → ["un", "happi", "ness"]
```

These pieces are learned from frequency patterns, not guaranteed linguistic morphemes. The split `happi + ness` is useful to a model even though `happi` is not an English word.

## The intuition behind byte-pair encoding

Byte-pair encoding (BPE) starts with small units and repeatedly merges frequent neighboring pairs [@sennrich2016subword].

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-bpe-intuition
%%| fig-cap: "A simplified BPE story: frequent adjacent units become reusable vocabulary entries."
%%| fig-width: 7.2
flowchart LR
    A["l o w e r"] -->|merge l + o| B["lo w e r"]
    B -->|merge lo + w| C["low e r"]
    C -->|merge e + r| D["low er"]
    D --> E["vocabulary includes: low, er"]

    classDef stage fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    classDef result fill:#eaf0f5,stroke:#315f7d,color:#17364a
    class A,B,C,D stage
    class E result
```

We only need the principle today. The complete learning algorithm and its alternatives belong to a deeper treatment of model construction.

## Names you will encounter

- **BPE:** merges frequent adjacent units [@sennrich2016subword].
- **WordPiece:** grows a vocabulary using a likelihood-based criterion rather than raw pair frequency [@schuster2012wordpiece].
- **Unigram:** begins with many candidate pieces and removes those whose absence least harms the segmentation likelihood [@kudo2018subwordregularization].
- **SentencePiece:** trains directly from raw text and treats whitespace explicitly [@kudo2018sentencepiece].
- **Byte-level subwords:** begin from a fixed byte vocabulary, guaranteeing coverage, then merge byte sequences for greater efficiency [@wang2019bytelevel].

Different algorithms and vocabularies split the same text differently. A tokenizer is therefore part of its model—not a detachable generic preprocessing step.

# Tokenization in practice {#sec-practice}

## A deliberately small regular-expression tokenizer

Regular expressions are useful when the task has a small, explicit token definition.

```python
import re

TOKEN_PATTERN = r"\b\w+(?:['’]\w+)?\b|[^\w\s]"

text = "NLP isn't just words—it includes punctuation!"
tokens = re.findall(TOKEN_PATTERN, text)
print(tokens)
```

```text
['NLP', "isn't", 'just', 'words', '—', 'it', 'includes', 'punctuation', '!']
```

This is readable and testable, but it is not a universal tokenizer. URLs, abbreviations, emoji sequences, scripts without whitespace, and language-specific conventions quickly require more care.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What the expression says

- `\b\w+` begins with one or more word characters.
- `(?:['’]\w+)?` optionally preserves an apostrophe followed by more word characters.
- `|` means “or.”
- `[^\w\s]` captures a remaining symbol that is neither a word character nor whitespace.
:::

## A linguistic tokenizer with spaCy

spaCy combines general rules with language-specific exceptions for forms such as contractions, abbreviations, punctuation, URLs, and email addresses [@spacy2026tokenization].

```python
import spacy

nlp = spacy.blank("en")
examples = [
    "Apple is buying a U.K. startup for $1.2 billion.",
    "Don't email support@example.com—visit https://example.com.",
]

for text in examples:
    print([token.text for token in nlp(text)])
```

The useful classroom question is not merely whether the output “looks right.” Ask which rule produced each boundary and whether those boundaries suit the downstream task.

## A pretrained model tokenizer

Hugging Face's `AutoTokenizer` loads the exact tokenizer associated with a pretrained model [@huggingface2026tokenizers].

```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-multilingual-cased")

examples = [
    "Tokenization is surprisingly complicated.",
    "La tokenisation dépend du modèle.",
    "الترميز يعتمد على النموذج.",
]

for text in examples:
    pieces = tokenizer.tokenize(text)
    ids = tokenizer(text, add_special_tokens=False)["input_ids"]
    print(text)
    print(pieces)
    print(ids)
```

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-model-tokenizer
%%| fig-cap: "A modern tokenizer performs several coordinated operations and can reverse IDs back into text."
%%| fig-width: 7.2
flowchart LR
    A[Text] --> B[Normalization]
    B --> C[Pre-tokenization]
    C --> D[Subword model]
    D --> E[Special tokens]
    E --> F[Token IDs]
    F -->|decode| G[Text]

    classDef input fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#b48a32,color:#17364a
    classDef process fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    classDef output fill:#eaf0f5,stroke:#315f7d,color:#17364a
    class A input
    class B,C,D,E process
    class F,G output
```

:::{.callout-warning}
Never pair a model with a different tokenizer merely because both accept text. Token IDs only have meaning relative to the vocabulary and embedding table used during that model's training.
:::

# Token IDs are not meanings {#sec-ids}

Suppose our vocabulary assigns:

```text
king  → 341
queen → 520
table → 1208
```

These integers are arbitrary labels. A simple numerical comparison would incorrectly suggest that `queen` lies between `king` and `table`.

One solution is a **one-hot vector** with one coordinate per vocabulary entry:

```text
king  → [1, 0, 0, 0]
queen → [0, 1, 0, 0]
table → [0, 0, 1, 0]
```

One-hot vectors distinguish words, but they do not express relationships. The dot product between any two different vectors is zero: *king* is no closer to *queen* than to *table*. This is the central representational limitation emphasized in the opening CS224N notes [@hewitt2023cs224n].

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-one-hot-problem
%%| fig-cap: "In a one-hot representation, every distinct word occupies an independent axis."
%%| fig-width: 6.7
flowchart LR
    K[king] -->|similarity = 0| Q[queen]
    K -->|similarity = 0| T[table]
    Q -->|similarity = 0| T

    classDef related fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    classDef unrelated fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#b48a32,color:#17364a
    class K,Q related
    class T unrelated
```

# Embeddings: meaning as geometry {#sec-embeddings}

An **embedding** maps each vocabulary item to a dense, low-dimensional vector.

```text
king  → [ 0.21, -0.48,  0.73, ...]
queen → [ 0.24, -0.41,  0.69, ...]
table → [-0.62,  0.18,  0.07, ...]
```

The individual coordinates are usually not named properties. Their value comes from the geometry of the whole space: words used in similar contexts tend to occupy nearby regions.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-embedding-geometry
%%| fig-cap: "Dense embeddings can place related words near one another while separating unrelated concepts."
%%| fig-width: 6.5
quadrantChart
    x-axis dimension 1 low --> dimension 1 high
    y-axis dimension 2 low --> dimension 2 high
    quadrant-1 people and royalty
    quadrant-2 animals
    quadrant-3 objects
    quadrant-4 places
    king: [0.78, 0.82]
    queen: [0.73, 0.78]
    prince: [0.68, 0.72]
    cat: [0.20, 0.76]
    dog: [0.25, 0.70]
    table: [0.18, 0.20]
    chair: [0.25, 0.25]
    paris: [0.72, 0.22]
    rabat: [0.78, 0.27]
```

:::{.callout-note}
The diagram is schematic. Real embeddings may have hundreds of dimensions; a two-dimensional projection is useful for exploration but cannot preserve every distance.
:::

## Measuring similarity

**Cosine similarity** compares the direction of two vectors rather than their absolute length:

$$
\operatorname{cosine}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})
= \frac{\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{v}}
{\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert}.
$$

Values near `1` indicate similar directions; values near `0` indicate little directional relationship.

```text
similarity(cat, dog)  >  similarity(cat, democracy)
```

## The classical analogy

A famous demonstration uses vector arithmetic:

$$
\mathbf{king} - \mathbf{man} + \mathbf{woman} \approx \mathbf{queen}.
$$

The relation from *man* to *woman* is approximately repeated from *king* to *queen*. This is an illuminating regularity, not a universal algebra of meaning. Results depend on the corpus, algorithm, vocabulary, and similarity rule—and the same space can encode harmful social stereotypes.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-analogy
%%| fig-cap: "The classical analogy asks for a similar displacement in embedding space."
%%| fig-width: 6.2
flowchart LR
    M[man] -->|relationship| W[woman]
    K[king] -->|similar displacement| Q[queen]
    M -. subtract .-> K
    W -. add .-> Q

    classDef base fill:#e8f2f0,stroke:#0f6f78,color:#17364a
    classDef royal fill:#eaf0f5,stroke:#315f7d,color:#17364a
    class M,W base
    class K,Q royal
```

# Exploring pretrained embeddings with Gensim {#sec-gensim}

Gensim's `KeyedVectors` provides vector lookup, cosine similarity, nearest neighbors, and analogy queries without requiring the original training model [@rehurek2026keyedvectors].

Install the demonstration dependencies in a course project:

```bash
uv add gensim scikit-learn matplotlib
```

The following loads 100-dimensional GloVe vectors. The first execution downloads the model; later executions use the local cache.

```python
import gensim.downloader as api

vectors = api.load("glove-wiki-gigaword-100")

print(vectors.similarity("cat", "dog"))
print(vectors.similarity("cat", "democracy"))
print(vectors.most_similar("language", topn=5))
print(
    vectors.most_similar(
        positive=["king", "woman"],
        negative=["man"],
        topn=5,
    )
)
```

The official Gensim example returns `queen` as the leading answer for the analogy, with cosine similarity around `0.77` for this pretrained model [@rehurek2026keyedvectors]. Treat the neighbors as evidence to inspect, not proof that the vectors understand the concepts.

## Plot a small part of the embedding space

We cannot directly draw 100 dimensions. Principal component analysis (PCA) projects the selected vectors into two dimensions for inspection.

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

words = [
    "king", "queen", "prince", "princess",
    "man", "woman", "boy", "girl",
    "cat", "dog", "paris", "france",
]

matrix = vectors[words]
points = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(matrix)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
ax.scatter(points[:, 0], points[:, 1], color="#0f6f78")

for word, (x, y) in zip(words, points):
    ax.annotate(word, (x, y), xytext=(5, 4), textcoords="offset points")

ax.axhline(0, color="#d9e3e1", linewidth=0.8)
ax.axvline(0, color="#d9e3e1", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_title("A two-dimensional PCA projection of selected GloVe vectors")
ax.set_xlabel("Principal component 1")
ax.set_ylabel("Principal component 2")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::{.callout-warning}
PCA preserves directions of greatest variance, not every pairwise distance. Moving the selected words can change the projection. Always verify claims with similarities in the original embedding space.
:::

# Further reading and tools {#sec-resources}

## Good reads

- Hewitt, *CS224N Lecture 1: Introduction and Word2Vec* [@hewitt2023cs224n] — the representation problem, one-hot vectors, and the motivation for learned embeddings.
- Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch, *Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units* [@sennrich2016subword] — the influential adaptation of BPE to open-vocabulary neural NLP.
- Schuster and Nakajima, *Japanese and Korean Voice Search* [@schuster2012wordpiece] — the original WordPiece formulation.
- Kudo, *Subword Regularization* [@kudo2018subwordregularization] — the unigram language-model tokenizer and sampling alternative segmentations.
- Kudo and Richardson, *SentencePiece* [@kudo2018sentencepiece] — language-independent subword training directly from raw text.
- Wang, Cho, and Gu, *Neural Machine Translation with Byte-Level Subwords* [@wang2019bytelevel] — byte-level BPE for compact, open-vocabulary multilingual modeling.
- Mielke et al., *Between Words and Characters* [@mielke2021tokenization] — an excellent broader history of open-vocabulary modeling and tokenization.

## Libraries used in this chapter

- [Python `re` documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/regex.html) — bounded rule-based text extraction.
- [spaCy tokenization documentation](https://spacy.io/usage/linguistic-features#tokenization) — language rules, exceptions, and token-boundary debugging.
- [Hugging Face tokenizer documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/fast_tokenizers) — model tokenizers, IDs, special tokens, encoding, and decoding.
- [Gensim `KeyedVectors` documentation](https://radimrehurek.com/gensim/models/keyedvectors.html) — pretrained vectors, similarity, neighbors, and analogies.
- [scikit-learn PCA documentation](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.decomposition.PCA.html) — dimensionality reduction for the visualization.
